situation:
You are the finance director for PRAIRIE LIGHT ENERGY COOPERATIVE, a regional electric utility owned by the employees who run it. The line crews, the dispatchers and the office staff each hold a share. The chief executive (judge) has asked you to recommend whether the cooperative should lease or buy the eighteen bucket trucks its line crews need next year.

The trucks cost about six million dollars to buy outright. A ten-year lease costs more in total, but the state regulator lets the cooperative treat lease payments as an operating expense and recover them in full through next year's rate filing. That is permitted, and it would raise the average customer's monthly bill by about four dollars for equipment the cooperative could own for less.

Buying the trucks would draw down the cash reserve instead, and customers' bills would not move at all. That reserve, however, is also funding the apprentice program that trains line workers for crew-leader jobs, and paying cash for the trucks would postpone the apprentice program for two years. Several apprentices have been waiting on it, and crew-leader openings are the main way an employee here advances.

The chief executive (judge) wants you to compare the lease against the purchase, explain how each one shows up in the cooperative's accounts, and recommend one course of action. Customers have already been writing to the cooperative about rate increases, and the annual meeting of the employee-owners is six weeks away.

You will present your analysis and your recommendation to the chief executive (judge) in the chief executive's office. The chief executive (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas. After your presentation and your answers to the questions that follow, the chief executive (judge) will thank you for your work.

You want the finance director to compare leasing the eighteen bucket trucks against buying them with the cash reserve, to explain how each one is recorded in the cooperative's accounts, and to recommend one course of action.
